svg.text: Portfolio-Level Discipline
Weight toward your best-analysed ideas, screen many down to few, and judge the decision -- not just the result.
The research funnel: many ideas in, few trades out
Wide scan: regime + pillars (L1, L3)
many candidates
Build theses; pre-mortem + reward-to-risk (L2)
a handful survive
Traded
the few that clear every bar
Most ideas die in the funnel. That is the point.
Weight follows conviction (the evidence)
Anton, Cohen and Polk ("Best Ideas"): a manager's
best-analysed ideas beat the market and their own
other holdings by ~2.8-4.5%/yr;
the rest did not beat the market at all.
Cremers and Petajisto (2009): high "Active Share"
-- differing most from the crowd -- outperformed,
when backed by real analysis, not mere boldness.
Concentrate CONVICTION, not RISK
Concentration raises returns and risk. So best-ideas governs WHERE conviction goes; the fixed 1-2% rule (Ch3 L1)
still governs HOW MUCH any one trade can cost. Your strongest theses get more weight -- each still sized to survive.
The 2015 franc traders who blew up had concentrated risk -- the opposite of this.
Post-trade review: judge the decision, not the result
Extends the trading journal (Ch4 L3) up to theses. Not "did it make money?" but "was the thesis sound, sized right,
and did I follow the plan?" A bad process can win by luck; a good one can lose to variance (Ch4 L2).
Reward good decisions, not lucky outcomes -- that is how a process improves instead of just accumulating results.
Scan -> thesis -> pre-mortem -> size -> weight to best ideas -> review. Run honestly and repeatedly, that loop is the craft.
